issues.legal_issue: Multiple principals may jointly appoint one agent through a common power of attorney.
material_facts: The plaintiff, his father, and his stepbrother jointly executed a power of attorney appointing one agent to act for them.
The challenge to the appointment relied on the fact that several principals had jointly granted the authority; no violation of contract law was shown.
issues.conclusion: The joint appointment of one agent by the three principals was legally permissible.
issues.legal_principle: Agency arises by contract when an agent has authority to act for a principal and consents to do so. Co-principals may jointly appoint an agent and become jointly liable to, and jointly sue, that agent. The Court relied on the general law of contract and Halsbury's Laws of England, Vol. 1, 4th ed., para. 726.

predicates.joint_agent_appointment_disputed: A challenge was made to the validity of appointing one agent for multiple principals.
predicates.multiple_principals_jointly_authorized_a: Multiple principals jointly authorized one agent to act for them.

issues.definition: When a challenged appointment was jointly made by multiple principals, the appointment is valid.

issues.legal_issue: The scope of a jointly granted power of attorney may extend to each principal's separate property where its terms and the circumstances show that intention.
material_facts: The principals each had separate lands and had no identified joint property, business, or venture.
They could not readily reach or manage their own lands and were contemplating migration.
They jointly granted the power of attorney for convenience, and the circumstances indicated that each wanted the agent to deal with his individual property.
The instrument used collective expressions such as acting on the principals' behalf.
issues.conclusion: The power of attorney authorized the agent to act in respect of each principal's individual property, not merely their joint affairs or property.
issues.legal_principle: The authority conferred by a power of attorney depends on its terms and the purpose for which it was executed, and the instrument is ordinarily construed strictly. Surrounding circumstances may nevertheless be considered to ascertain the parties' intention. The Court relied on Bryant, Powis and Bryant Ltd. v. La Banque du Peuple, 1893 A.C. 170 at 177, and Modi & Co. v. Union of India, [1963] 2 S.C.R. 565.

predicates.scope_of_joint_power_disputed: A dispute arose over whether a jointly granted authority covered only joint affairs or also separate affairs.
predicates.principals_owned_separate_properties: The principals each owned property separately rather than holding only joint property.
predicates.principals_could_not_manage_their_proper: The principals could not readily access or manage their separate properties.
predicates.circumstances_show_individual_dealing_pu: The circumstances surrounding the appointment showed that each principal intended the agent to deal with that principal's own property.

issues.definition: Where a disputed joint authority concerns principals with separate properties who cannot manage them and the circumstances show an individual-dealing purpose, the authority covers each principal's separate property.

issues.legal_issue: A general power of attorney is not invalid merely because the registrar omitted an endorsement identifying or confirming the identity of its executants.
material_facts: The principals admitted executing the power of attorney.
The registrar's endorsement did not state that the executants were personally known to the registrar or had been identified by someone known to the registrar.
No rule requiring such an endorsement was identified.
issues.conclusion: The omission of the identification endorsement did not invalidate the power of attorney.
issues.legal_principle: A general power of attorney is not compulsorily registrable, and the Court found no legal obligation requiring the registrar to endorse that the executants were personally known or identified by a known person. Where execution is admitted, the omission does not invalidate the deed.

rule.if: instrument_validity_disputed and general_power_of_attorney and execution_admitted and registrar_omitted_identity_endorsement

predicates.instrument_validity_disputed: A party challenged whether an instrument was legally valid.
predicates.general_power_of_attorney: The disputed instrument was a general authority for an agent to act for its executants.
predicates.execution_admitted: The persons who executed the instrument admitted doing so.
predicates.registrar_omitted_identity_endorsement: The registrar did not endorse that the executants were personally known or identified by a person known to the registrar.

issues.definition: If execution of a disputed general authority is admitted, the registrar's omission of an identity endorsement does not invalidate the document.

issues.legal_issue: An agent has authority to sell property when the power of attorney expressly grants that authority.
material_facts: The power of attorney expressly referred to purchasing and selling lands and executing and registering sale deeds.
The supplementary instrument also confirmed the power to sell and register sale documents.
issues.conclusion: The agent was expressly authorized to sell the principals' lands.
issues.legal_principle: The authority granted by a power of attorney is determined by its terms and the instrument must be read as a whole. The Court relied on the express sale language in the instruments and referred to Halsbury's Laws of England, 4th ed., Vol. 1, para. 733, in explaining that ordinary authority expressly granted in one part is not cut down by ambiguous or uncertain expressions elsewhere.

predicates.agent_sale_authority_disputed: A party disputed whether an agent had authority to sell property.
predicates.instrument_expressly_authorized_property: The written authority expressly empowered the agent to sell the relevant kind of property.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns an agent's sale authority and the written authority expressly permits property sales, the agent is authorized to sell the property.

issues.legal_issue: An express power to sell is not restricted to financing litigation or repaying litigation-related borrowing unless the instrument makes that restriction a condition of sale.
material_facts: The power of attorney separately recited authority to sell land, authority to conduct litigation, and authority to borrow money or pay debts.
The instrument did not state that land could be sold only to finance litigation or repay a loan taken for that purpose.
issues.conclusion: The authority to sell land was not limited to financing litigation or repaying a related loan.
issues.legal_principle: A document must be considered as a whole, but separate grants of authority remain independent unless the wording makes one conditional on another. The Court relied on Halsbury's Laws of England, 4th ed., Vol. 1, para. 733.

predicates.sale_power_restriction_disputed: A party claimed that an agent's power to sell property was restricted to a particular purpose.
predicates.instrument_separately_granted_sale_autho: The instrument recited authority to sell property separately from other authorities.
predicates.instrument_separately_granted_other_powe: The instrument also granted other powers, such as conducting litigation or borrowing money.
predicates.no_language_made_sale_conditional: The instrument did not make the sale authority conditional on carrying out another purpose.

issues.definition: If a document separately grants sale authority and other powers without making sale conditional on another purpose, the sale authority is not limited to that purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A property owner who acquiesces in a sale by an ostensible owner and accepts the consideration may not later challenge the transferee's title on the ground that the ostensible owner lacked authority.
material_facts: The plaintiff's father acted as though he owned the land and entered into an agreement to sell it.
The sale was completed for consideration, which the evidence showed was paid to and accepted by the plaintiff in his presence.
The plaintiff knew of and acquiesced in the transaction.
The plaintiff later challenged the sale on the basis that his father lacked authority and the agent had merely completed a sale negotiated by another person.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff was estopped from challenging the title transferred through the sale, and the challenge to the transferee's title failed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, protects a transfer for consideration by an ostensible owner where the person interested in the property consented expressly or impliedly to that appearance of ownership. The Court also applied the equitable principle recognized in Ramcoomar v. Macqueen, (1872) I.A. 11, Bengal L.R. 46, and held that acquiescence and acceptance of consideration estopped the plaintiff from contesting the sale.

rule.if: transferee_title_challenged and another_person_acted_as_ostensible_owner and interested_owner_acquiesced_in_sale and interested_owner_accepted_sale_consideration

predicates.transferee_title_challenged: A person challenged the title acquired by a transferee through a property sale.
predicates.another_person_acted_as_ostensible_owner: Another person acted toward others as though that person owned the property.
predicates.interested_owner_acquiesced_in_sale: The person with an interest in the property knew of and acquiesced in the sale.
predicates.interested_owner_accepted_sale_considera: The person with an interest in the property accepted the consideration paid for the sale.

issues.definition: When an interested owner acquiesces in a sale by someone acting as owner and accepts the sale consideration, the owner is barred from challenging the transferee's title.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may admit additional evidence when it requires that evidence to pronounce judgment, but a party has no right to produce additional evidence merely by seeking to do so.
material_facts: In an appeal, the High Court allowed registered sale deeds to be produced although they had not been produced at trial.
The High Court gave reasons for finding the deeds necessary to enable it to pronounce judgment.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had properly exercised its discretion.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had jurisdiction to admit the sale deeds, and its decision to do so was not disturbed.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, does not confer a right on a party to introduce additional evidence. An appellate court may permit additional evidence when it requires a document to enable it to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause; a properly exercised discretionary decision may be left undisturbed.

predicates.appeal_in_appellate_court: The proceeding is an appeal being heard by an appellate court.
predicates.party_seeks_additional_evidence: A party asks to introduce evidence that was not produced earlier.
predicates.appellate_court_requires_evidence_to_pro: The appellate court considers the evidence necessary to enable it to decide the appeal.
predicates.appellate_court_properly_exercises_discr: The appellate court gives a proper basis for exercising its discretion to admit the evidence.

issues.definition: In an appeal, additional evidence may be admitted when the appellate court needs it to decide the case and properly exercises its discretion.

issues.legal_issue: A person named as transferee is not a benamidar merely because another person may have influenced the grant of the property when no consideration for the transfer is shown to have come from that other person.
material_facts: The land was granted by the ruler and the patta was issued in the plaintiff's name while he was a minor.
The plaintiff's father held high office and may have influenced the grant, but no evidence showed that the patta was issued for consideration or that consideration flowed from the father.
The defendants claimed that the plaintiff was a benamidar for his father.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff was not established to be a benamidar.
issues.legal_principle: Section 82 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, applies where property is transferred to one person for consideration paid or provided by another who did not intend the consideration as a benefit to the transferee. The Court stated that benami requires consideration to flow from one person while title is taken in another's name, without an intention to make a gift to the named transferee. Those ingredients were absent.

predicates.benami_status_disputed: A party disputed whether the person named as property holder was a benamidar for someone else.
predicates.property_named_in_claimants_name: The property was granted or recorded in the name of the person asserting ownership.
predicates.no_consideration_shown_from_alleged_bene: No evidence showed that the person alleged to be the real beneficial owner paid or provided consideration for the property.

issues.definition: When benami status is disputed, property is named in the claimant's name, and no consideration is shown to have come from the alleged beneficial owner, benami status is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A compromise with some defendants does not make an appeal against other transferees infructuous when the claim against them independently concerns the agent's authority and the title acquired through the transfers.
material_facts: The plaintiff compromised the appeal against some defendants, including the alleged participants in the fraud.
The appeal remained against other defendants who had acquired property through sales made by the agent.
The claim against those remaining defendants rested on the scope of the agent's authority and the transferees' acquisition of title.
issues.conclusion: The compromise did not render the appeal against the remaining defendants infructuous or untenable.
issues.legal_principle: A compromise with some defendants does not dispose of an independent claim against other transferees where the claim concerns the authority under which their transfers were made and the title they acquired.

predicates.appeal_against_remaining_transferees: An appeal remains pending against transferees other than the defendants with whom a compromise was reached.
predicates.compromise_with_some_defendants: The appellant compromised or withdrew the appeal against some defendants.
predicates.claim_against_remaining_transferees_inde: The claim against the remaining transferees independently concerns their title or the authority for the transfers to them.

issues.definition: If an appellant compromises with some defendants but maintains an independent title claim against other transferees, the appeal against those transferees remains maintainable.
